title: Chapter 84 – Moon-Ash
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Jian]

Overseer Han counts the roots twice, and then he counts them a third time, aloud, with his abacus.

"Two," he says. "Two Earthheart, drawn whole, no iron, no tear." He taps the bone tongs on the table. "The Pill Hall's apprentice has clean hands."

It is the afternoon of the twenty-eighth day. The party stands in the Overseer's office at the foot of Medicine Valley, a low timber room that smells of sulfur and old tea, with a window on the terraces and a rack of dried leaves along one wall. Feng sits on a bench with his leg propped on a stool and Wei Chen's jade splints still on it. Tan Ruyan stands upright by the door with a white jade box under her arm. Zhao Yao hovers behind her, gray with fatigue. Jian holds his satchel against his chest.

"The boar," says Han.

"Dead, Overseer. Second-rank, male, old. Killed by the team." Tan Ruyan lays the evidence on the table: two tusks, a strip of hide, a small stoppered vial of dark gold. "Marrow harvested. One for the leader, one for the Hall, per the warrant."

"The vine."

"Cut." It is Wei Chen who answers, quietly. "Nine stems. By bone or glass, two days before the party arrived. I have written the report."

The Overseer does not move. For the length of three breaths, the red face holds perfectly still. Then he lets out a long slow exhale through his nose, and sits down heavily in the chair behind the table, and puts his hands over his eyes.

"Nine," he says. "In thirty years nobody has cut the Marrow Vine. Nobody knew where it was." He drops his hands. His eyes are small and bright and very tired. "Who did?"

"We do not know, Overseer."

"You found no sign."

"A footprint," says Wei Chen. "And iron ink. And a thread."

"A thread."

"In the beasts' throats, Overseer. Black, stitched, wound three times. I have seen it in forty-one of the dead boars, and in the old male." Wei Chen takes a small folded cloth from his sleeve and lays it on the table. In the cloth is a coil of black cord, no longer than a finger. "It is the same cord that held the Deacon's face."

Han looks at it for a long moment. He does not touch it.

"You will take this to Duan."

"I have asked for a messenger, Overseer."

"Good." Han straightens his shoulders. "I will write a letter to go with it. I will say that the Medicine Valley asks for the Hall's protection, and that I will close the upper terraces until I have it. And I will say," he adds, in a voice that has gone quite flat, "that I never believed it was the snow."

* * *

Jian waits until the others have gone.

He stands by the window with his satchel in his arms and watches Tan Ruyan cross the yard in the thin gold light, with her spear on her shoulder and her white box carried carefully. Zhao Yao follows. Feng goes out on Wei Chen's arm, grim and silent. The office empties. The Overseer is left alone with his abacus, a pile of reports, and a boy who has not moved.

"There is something else," says Han, without looking up.

"The pool, Overseer."

"What about it?"

"In the cleft. A black pool, thirty paces across, with a ledge. There were lotus in it." Jian chooses his words. "Nine buds. They did not look like ordinary lotus. They were gray at the edge. I think they were Moon-ash."

The brush stops.

"I did not touch them," says Jian. "The mission was for roots and marrow. But I have read the Pill Hall's scroll. Moon-ash lotus is one of the five reagents of a Level 1 pill called the Nine Turn. It is a body-and-Qi stabilizer. It is taught to no one, because the lotus is rare." He keeps his hands still on the satchel. "If the vine was cut two days before we arrived, I think the lotus may be next."

Han puts down the brush.

"They are the Valley's," he says slowly. "They bloom once a year, on the third night after the new moon. They are ash by dawn." He looks at Jian. "I have a registry. I have a quota. Nobody has asked for Moon-ash in my time."

"I am asking, Overseer."

"For what?"

"For the Pill Hall. Elder Bai is old. He would like to try the Nine Turn before he dies." It is a lie, and a clean one; Bai would, in fact, like that. "One bud, for the Hall. And one for the apprentice who found it."

"Two."

"Two."

The Overseer is silent. His thumb moves on the edge of the abacus. Outside, a bird calls in the dusk, and it takes Jian a moment to understand why the sound is strange: it is the first he has heard in the Valley in ten days. The beasts, he thinks, are beginning to return.

"It is the third night after the new moon," says Han, at last.

"Yes, Overseer."

"Tonight."

"I know."

"You count well." The red face crinkles into something almost like a smile. "Two buds. One to the Hall, one to you. I will take twenty points from your reward, because I must take something. And you will carry them in a box of cold jade, with no iron, and you will not drop it." He opens a drawer and takes out a small box of pale green stone. "I am too old to be sorry for a thing I have done for a good reason."

Jian takes the box.

It is cold in his hand. It weighs almost nothing.

Tan Ruyan is waiting on the steps outside, with the white box under her arm and the last of the sun on her face.

"Two lotus," she says. "From a man who has not given a lotus in thirty years."

"You were listening."

"I was standing at the window. It is not the same." She does not smile. "I have the marrow. I have a root, half of the Overseer's allowance, which he gave me because I asked him politely. I am short the powder, the dew and the cinnabar. So are you." She looks out over the terraces. "The Inner Sect trial is in forty days. The winners receive a badge. A badge opens the red slips."

"I know."

"I mean to win it." Her eyes come back to his, level and clear. "I wanted you to hear it from me. You will not enter. You are an Outer disciple of one month, and the trial is for the eighth layer and above, and there will be nothing in it for an apprentice of the Pill Hall. But you will be somewhere near it, because you are always somewhere near the thing I am doing." A short breath that is almost a laugh. "I do not mind. I would only like us to be clear."

"We are clear."

"Good." She shifts the box. "I will tell you one thing, because you gave me a fair share. The auction on the fifteenth. My family has a stall there. I can bid for the powder under the Tan name, and it will cost me less than it would cost you." She turns and goes down the steps. "Think about what you can trade me for it."

He watches her go, small and straight and gold in the failing light.

She is not an enemy, he thinks. She is a competitor. It is a very different thing.

* * *

The next thing he does is tell Deputy Rong about the knots.

He does it in the Enforcement Hall's outer room, standing, with his hat in his hand. The Deputy's tablet is open on the table before him. He listens with his gray mustache bristling, and his small gray eyes never leave Jian's face.

"A knot," says Rong. "Under the rail of a cot."

"Reed Courtyard, number six. The left rail, at the head, on the underside, in the join of the wood. It is a three-loop tie in black thread." Jian describes it. "I found it on the night of the Register. I did not know what it was. I thought it was a watcher's mark."

"You did not report it."

"I did not know to whom. And I thought," he says carefully, "that if the Hall wished to find it, it would."

Rong makes a small noise in his throat. It might be a laugh. He writes something and turns the tablet. "You will understand that this is a very irregular thing to report on the twenty-eighth day. Almost a month after the event."

"Yes, Deputy."

"It is also the first lead I have had since the Deacon's face came off."

He rises. He goes to the door and says a few words to the clerk outside, and the clerk goes off at a trot. When Rong returns, he stands for a moment with his arms folded and his chin lowered, like a man doing arithmetic.

"If it was done in a courtyard of boys, it was done in others." His mustache twitches. "I shall have the courtyards searched. All of them. Tonight. The Hall will say it is a sweep for contraband." He pauses. "You will not mention that you told me."

"I will not."

"Good." The Deputy sits down again. "You do realize, Disciple, that a boy who finds a Blood Shadow's knot under his own bed and says nothing for a month is a boy I would very much like to have a long, quiet talk with."

Everyone says that.

"I am ten, Deputy," says Jian. "I am not a very interesting person."

"No," says Rong, unsmiling. "You are the most interesting person I have met in twenty years. It is why I find you tiresome." He turns the page. "Go and sleep. And tell your friend the Zhao boy to be careful with his brother."

Jian goes still.

"I have a clerk in the Outer Affairs Hall," says Rong, "who keeps the courier ledger. A letter went out two days ago to the Lin clan of Green Pine Hill. Another is expected back. I am not a fool, Disciple. I read ledgers." He does not look up. "You will find that I am on your side. It is not a comfortable thing to be told. I would not mention it."

* * *

The sweep takes four hours, and by the end of it, the refectory has the whole story.

Jian arrives at the back door at the second hour of the night with snow on his shoulders, to find Reed Courtyard's eight boys huddled round a long table with blankets and a pot of tea, and Ma Bao in the middle of a speech. His cheerful broad face is flushed. His cut chin is bandaged. He has not stopped talking since the Hall's men took the beds.

"Eleven," he is saying. "My cousin counted. Eleven, in six courtyards. Not just ours. Under rails, behind shutters, one in the latrine." He lowers his voice to a dramatic whisper. "Black thread. Tied in little knots. Rong held one up with a pair of tongs and the clerk dropped his pen."

"Eleven knots," says Pei, wide-eyed.

"In six courtyards." Ma Bao looks around the table, tremendously pleased. "Somebody has been going from bed to bed for a month, tying them. And nobody saw."

Jian sits. A bowl of tea is put in his hands. He drinks it, and says nothing, and watches the boy at the end of the table.

Lan Tong sits with his knees drawn up and a blanket over his shoulders. He is looking at the fire. His face is pale and shut, as always, but his fingers are moving. They are folding something, a dry brown leaf, with the quick patient neatness of a person who has done it a thousand times. He folds it in half. He folds it in half again. He lays it on the bench, a small neat square, and when he glances up and finds Jian watching, his eyes do not drop.

He pushes the square across the wood.

Jian does not take it at once. He waits until Ma Bao has begun a new story, about a dog in the Beast Hall that ate a Deacon's shoe. Then he draws the folded leaf into his palm, below the table's edge, and puts it in his sleeve with the other two.

Three leaves.

He has kept them all. He has not known what to do with them.

* * *

By the time the courtyards are searched, the thirtieth night has come.

Jian does not see it. He is on Terrace Nine at the hour of the dog, in the dark, in the snow, with a pangolin on his shoulder and a box of cold jade in his hands. Below him the Court lies under a sky so clear it hurts. The new moon is three nights old. A thin pale sickle hangs just above the western ridge. The stars crowd round it. The air is so cold that the breath hangs in front of his face and does not move.

Reed Courtyard has been emptied for the sweep. Rong's men have turned out the cots and rolled up the straw. Ma Bao grumbled. Pei wept. In the end all eight boys were sent to the refectory with blankets and a pot of tea, and Jian slipped out of the back.

Day 30, says the line in the corner of his sight.

It is the first time it has changed in weeks. The gray letters have gone pale, and begun, very slightly, to flicker. Beneath the date a second line has appeared, thin and cold, in the same dim ash color:

```
Restart condition met: Day 30.
Ritual required: Moon-ash.
Place: open sky. Host: alone.
Procedure: burn 1 bud. Inhale the ash. Press right palm to earth.
Duration: until restart.
```

He reads it three times. Then he sits down on the snow under the old pine.

Alone. He has not told the others, and has not wished to. He has Pebble, who is not a witness, and who has been given a stern talk about the importance of staying very still. The pangolin has gone down from his shoulder to sit at his knee, with all its scales up and its eyes on the box.

He opens the lid.

There are two buds. They lie on a bed of damp moss, each the size of a fist, and each as gray as ash. They are closed. But as he breathes on them, a faint pale glow runs along the edge of the petals, and the air in front of his face smells suddenly of rain on cold stone. It is a clean smell. It is the smell of something very old.

One for the ritual. One for the Nine Turn.

He takes the leaves out before he strikes the flint.

He does not know why. He has been carrying them in his sleeve for three weeks: three dry brown leaves folded in four, soft as cloth at the creases, each the length of his palm. He spreads them on his knee in the starlight. They are nothing, he had thought. A boy's gesture. A scrap of kindness from a silent child.

Now he smells them.

Rain on cold stone.

He sets one beside the open box. The leaf and the bud are the same gray. They have the same fine veins, running outward from the stem like the ribs of a fan. They have the same smell. He lifts the leaf to the moon and sees, in the pale light, a faint dark pattern pressed into the folds: a seven-lobed ring, drawn with a thorn.

Lan Tong knew.

He sits very still. The silent boy of Reed Courtyard, who has not spoken a word in two months, who watches from his cot with eyes like a cat's, who left a moon-ash leaf under a stranger's pillow before there was any reason in the world for a stranger to need one. Who has folded a ring into a leaf, three times, and pushed it across a table.

Who is he?

There is no answer. There is only the wind in the pine, and the small hot weight of the pangolin on his knee, and the gray bud under his hand. He puts the leaves away.

He takes the left bud in his fingers. It is cool and soft and light as a feather. He sets it in a little hollow he has scraped in the snow, between the roots of the pine. From his sleeve he takes the flint he borrowed from Gu, and the small steel, and strikes a spark.

It catches at once.

The bud does not burn as wood burns. It crumbles. A pale silver flame runs up its petals and the whole thing sinks into itself, soft as a sigh, and in an instant it is a heap of fine gray dust, glowing faintly at the heart like an ember. A wisp of smoke rises. It does not drift. It stands upright in the windless dark, a thin white thread, and curls at the top, and bends toward his face.

Inhale.

He leans forward and breathes in.

* * *

It tastes of nothing. It tastes of cold water. It goes down his throat like a drink of snow and spreads through his chest in a slow silver wave, and where it passes, the dark inside him begins to move.

He puts his right palm flat on the earth.

The ground is frozen hard. It does not yield. But beneath the hardness, a hand's depth down, he feels a heartbeat. It is slow and vast and patient: the pulse of a mountain, six hundred years old, under a mantle of snow. It is the same pulse he felt on the fortieth landing. It runs up through the frost into his palm and climbs his arm and meets the silver in his chest.

There.

The pain begins.

It is not the pain of the dock. That was a tearing; this is a kindling. A thin line of heat runs up his spine, vertebra by vertebra, as if someone were lighting a row of lamps. At the base of the skull it flares. His eyes snap wide. He sees, for one instant, a corridor of white squares unrolled across the night, and at the far end of it, small and distant and very bright, a door.

It opens.

The darkness in the corner of his sight breaks like ice. A soft white light floods in, clean, pure and without color. It is not the dim ash of the last thirty days. It is the old light, the light of the panel, the light he has not seen since the landing. But it is different. It is not a rectangle. It has no border. It unrolls across his sight in a slow, circular wave, ring on ring, as a pond ripples round a thrown stone.

At its center a seven-lobed shape forms. It is white, and then silver, and then a pale warm gold.

His mouth is open. He is breathing in short gasps. Beside him Pebble has risen on its hind legs, scales flared, and a high thin sound comes from its throat, not a cry, not a word, but a note, the long bright note of a creature that has heard a bell rung in a house it thought was empty.

```
ARK-7 INTERFACE — RESTART COMPLETE.
Cradle integration: CONFIRMED.
Interface Level: 3 (cradle-extended).
Scan: ONLINE (calibration pending).
Fabrication: ONLINE.
Synthesis: ONLINE. Ceiling: Level 2 pills.
Seam-sight: ONLINE.
Restart gift: +50 CE.
CE: 0 -> 50.
```

He stares at it.

He had not known how much he would feel it. He had known he would miss it. He had known it would be strange. But the relief that rises in him is so large and so sudden that for a moment he cannot see, and finds that his cheeks are wet, and wipes them on his sleeve.

Thirty days.

He thinks of the dropped pestle. The walk into the door. The long nights in the dead yard, hitting a post with a stick, and Feng's voice in the dark. Whatever you have lost, you have not lost the part that matters. He thinks of the old man in the furnace room who said, with his hand on the latch, tell me whether it was worth the price.

It was.

He does not know if it is true. But it is what he thinks, kneeling in the snow, and he holds it.

* * *

The changes come in a slow bright flood, line by line.

```
NEW FACE — NOTES
Interface layout updated. Panel border removed. Seven-lobe anchor displayed.
All functions retained. Functions modified:

SCAN:
First Scan after restart: calibration cost x3.
Subsequent Scans: normal cost.
Scan Structure (items, pills): now returns full material chain on recognition.

SYNTHESIS:
Ceiling raised: Level 1 -> Level 2 pills.
Requires: all reagents + CE.
Note: formula "Foundation Establishment Pill (Level 2)" recorded from scan. Status: reagents 3/5.

SEAM-SIGHT:
Passive. Range extended. Cost: none.

ADDITIONAL:
Cradle dock: linked. Anchor: Hundred Stairs, landing 40.
Anchor status: DORMANT. Awaiting host (Foundation).
```

He reads it slowly.

Reagents held: two of five. The Earthheart root, and the marrow. The jade powder waits for the auction. The dew and the cinnabar wait behind a red seal. He counts them off against the panel's line, and the count comes out right.

Beneath it, in a corner he had not noticed before, the panel has begun to keep another list.

```
REGISTERED FORMULAS (known):
1. Foundation Establishment Pill (Level 2) — 5 reagents, 1 fire sequence, 1 resonance step.
2. Nine Turn Pill (Level 1, peak) — 5 reagents (Ninefold marrow vine, Moon-ash lotus, Heartroot, Frostbell, Mourner's cup). Hand-brewing permitted (Rank 1 limit).
Held: lotus 1/1. Marrow vine 0/1 (source: tenth stem, hidden cleft, Valley-reserved).
```

The Nine Turn. He has not scanned it. The Interface has recorded it from somewhere. From Qinghe's slips, perhaps, or from the Pill Hall's scroll, or from the long dim memory of the Garden. It knows.

Everything I learned, it kept.

He breathes out.

He is weak. He is cold to the bone. But there is a sudden spreading warmth in his chest, and the world, when he looks up, comes apart along its seams: the pine behind him, a lattice of ring on ring; the snow, a scatter of crystals; the mountain beneath, a vast slow spiral that descends and descends into the dark. Far below, on the fortieth landing, a seven-lobed ring of light pulses once, like a heart.

The dock is awake.

* * *

He is packing the ashes when the last thing appears.

He has gathered what is left of the bud into a twist of paper: a pinch of fine gray dust, still faintly warm. He does not know why. It seems wrong to leave it. He folds the paper and puts it in his sleeve. Pebble has curled up in his lap, exhausted, with its nose under its tail. The moon has moved a hand's width across the sky.

The panel, which has been quiet, brightens.

It does not flicker or ring. It merely grows, a little, the way a window grows when the sun rises behind it. The seven-lobed shape at its center turns once and settles. And beneath it, in letters that are not gray or white but a clear, warm gold, a new line appears.

It is not a report. It is not a notice. It is not a warning or a prompt.

It is a greeting.

```
Welcome back, Gardener.
```
